children.name: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
children.blurb: This page covers how copyright and trademark law applies to works created with or by AI, including images, text, music, and video.

sections.body: This field covers the legal and practical questions around who owns AI-generated work, what rights attach to it, and how creators can prove where a piece came from. Artificial intelligence is now being used to generate images, video, and audio, and the rights and provenance section explains the rules that apply to that output. It looks at copyright and trademark questions, the terms under which synthetic media can be licensed, and the ways training data is collected and contested. It also covers the security measures studios use to protect their work and the technical systems that attach credentials or watermarks to files. The focus is on what is actually happening in law and practice, not on what might happen in theory.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work in this area is unsettled. Copyright protection for purely AI-generated material is not clearly established in many places, and courts and registries are still working through how human authorship applies. Licensing models for synthetic media are developing, but there is no single standard that everyone follows. Training data and opt-out mechanisms exist, yet they are uneven and often hard for individual artists to enforce. Studio security is a real concern, but the tools available range from basic access controls to more advanced monitoring, and none are foolproof. Watermarking and content credentials are technically possible, but they can be removed or stripped, and adoption is far from universal. This site currently tracks no active intellectual property lawsuits, so no case names or outcomes are reported here.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to know whether they can claim rights in an AI image should start with Copyright and Trademark for AI Work, which explains the basic legal tests and the limits of protection. If they plan to sell or reuse synthetic media, Licensing Synthetic Media walks through the terms and restrictions that commonly appear in those agreements. Training Data and Opt-Outs is the page for anyone concerned about whether their own work was used to train a model and what they can do about it. Security for Creative Studios covers the practical steps a studio can take to keep prompts, drafts, and finished assets from leaking or being misused. Finally, Watermarking and Content Credentials explains the technical markers that can travel with a file and what they can and cannot prove about its origin.
